name: Swiggy
summary: Swiggy's engineering interviews usually mix problem-solving rounds, a machine coding or low-level design round and, for experienced roles, system design, with design topics often drawn from real-time delivery: tracking, dispatch and delivery-time estimates. Swiggy publishes its values, such as Consumer Comes First, Display a Founder Mentality and Stand-up & Disagree but Commit Fully, and candidates commonly report hiring manager rounds that probe ownership and speed.
looks_for: Always be Curious, Always be Learning
Move Fast, Break Barriers and Deliver Results

questions.text: How would you design order tracking for a food-delivery app?
covers: The order's states (placed, accepted, picked up, delivered) and who updates each
Getting the partner's live location to the customer: update rate, push versus polling, battery
What the customer sees when data is late or a partner's phone goes offline

questions.text: Tell me about a time you shipped something fast. What trade-offs did you make?
covers: Why speed mattered, in terms of users or the business
What you cut or simplified, and what you refused to cut
What you fixed or finished after launch

questions.text: Tell me about a feature you built that users loved.
covers: The user problem it solved, and how you knew it was a real problem
Your part in building it
How you knew users loved it: usage, ratings or feedback, ideally with a number

questions.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision, said so, and then committed to it fully.
covers: Your view and the evidence behind it
How and to whom you raised it
How you backed the final decision in practice, and how it turned out

questions.text: Describe a time you delivered something useful with fewer people, less time or less money than you wanted.
covers: The constraint and what the full version would have needed
How you simplified the problem or reused what existed
What you delivered and what it achieved

questions.text: Tell me about feedback that was hard to hear. What did you change because of it?
covers: The feedback, stated plainly, and who gave it
Your first reaction and how you checked whether it was fair
A concrete change in how you work since

questions.text: How would you assign incoming orders to delivery partners in a busy area at dinner time?
covers: Inputs: partner locations, restaurant preparation time, distance and current load
The goal you optimise: delivery time versus partner idle time, and when to batch two orders
What happens when a partner rejects or goes offline, and fairness in how work is shared

questions.text: How would you estimate the delivery time shown to a customer before they place an order?
covers: Splitting it into parts: preparation, partner reaching the restaurant, travel to the customer
Data for each part: past orders by restaurant and time, traffic, weather
Measuring accuracy, updating the estimate live, and the cost of promising too little or too much

questions.text: How would you keep stock accurate in a quick-commerce app that serves customers from many small stores?
covers: A source of truth per store, updated on orders, picking and restocking
Holding items at checkout so two customers don't buy the last one
Handling mismatches found while picking: substitutes, partial refunds, alerts

questions.text: Payments in one city start failing during a cricket final. Walk me through your first 30 minutes.
covers: Confirming scope on dashboards: which city, payment method or gateway, since when
Mitigating first: routing to another gateway, switching off a heavy feature
Keeping others informed, then a blameless review of the cause

questions.text: Explain the trade-offs between polling, WebSockets and push notifications for live updates in a mobile app.
covers: Polling: simple but wasteful; WebSockets: live but many open connections to manage
Push notifications for when the app is in the background
Battery and data use on low-end phones and patchy networks

questions.text: Repeat orders from new users in one city fell last month. How would you find out why?
covers: Checking the data first, then splitting by area, platform and first-order experience
Likely causes: late deliveries, fees, fewer restaurants, a competitor's offer
The most likely cause and how you'd test a fix

questions.text: Why Swiggy? Which of Swiggy's values fits how you like to work?
covers: A reason tied to the product or the problems, not only the brand
One value, named once, with a short example from your work
What you hope to learn or build here

questions.text: Which part of Swiggy (food delivery, Instamart or dining out) would you like to work on, and what would you improve first?
covers: A clear pick and why it interests you
One specific improvement for customers, restaurants, stores or delivery partners
How you'd measure whether it worked

tips: Real-time systems (tracking, dispatch, ETAs) are favourite design topics.
Swiggy groups its published values into heart, head and hands; prepare a story each for consumer focus, founder mentality and disagree-and-commit.
For machine coding, get a working version running early, then refactor into clear classes, and leave time to walk the interviewer through it.
In design answers, cover everyone the system serves: customers, restaurant partners and delivery partners.
Mention cheap phones and patchy networks when you talk about the apps; it shows you're thinking about real users across India.

sources.title: What We Value at Swiggy (Swiggy Diaries)
